claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis, though the difference did not reach statistical significance.

claims.claim: The distribution of mEPSC amplitude was significantly different between fasted and fed groups.
claims.source: The distribution of amplitude was significantly different between fasted and fed groups (p<0.001, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test) (Figure 1d).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Postsynaptic properties may be altered in POMC neurons in animals undergoing changes in their energy states.
claims.source: These data indicate that postsynaptic properties may be altered in POMC neurons in animals undergoing changes in their energy states.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the mEPSC data presented.

claims.claim: The AMPAR/NMDAR ratio showed no significant difference between POMC neurons of fasted and fed animals.
claims.source: There was no significant difference between POMC neurons of fasted and fed animals (fasting, 1.672 ± 0.679, n = 6; feeding, 1.415 ± 0.136, n = 6, p=0.73, T-test) (Figure 2d).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: The eEPSC exhibited a significant increase in the rectification of the current-voltage (I-V) relationship of AMPARs in POMC neurons of fed mice compared to fasted animals.
claims.source: However, the eEPSC recorded in the presence of NMDAR inhibitor, AP5 (50 µM) and GABAA receptor inhibitor, bicuculline (30 µM) exhibited a significant increase in the rectification of the current-voltage (I-V) relationship of AMPARs in POMC neurons of fed mice compared to fasted animals (Figure 2a,b).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing I-V relationships.

claims.claim: The RI of AMPAR-EPSC in POMC neurons was 0.59 ± 0.01 (n = 8) in fasted mice and 0.30 ± 0.03 (n = 7) in fed mice (p<0.05, unpaired t-test).
claims.source: The RI of AMPAR-EPSC in POMC neurons was 0.59 ± 0.01 (n = 8) in fasted mice and 0.30 ± 0.03 (n = 7) in fed mice (p<0.05, unpaired t-test) (Figure 2c)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: The rectification of AMPAR-EPSCs was more significant in fed mice than in fasted ones.
claims.source: The RI of AMPAR-EPSC in POMC neurons was 0.59 ± 0.01 (n = 8) in fasted mice and 0.30 ± 0.03 (n = 7) in fed mice (p<0.05, unpaired t-test) (Figure 2c), indicating that the rectification of AMPAR-EPSCs was more significant in fed mice than in fasted ones.
claims.evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the RI data.

claims.claim: Fasting facilitates GluR2-containing AMPAR translocation to synapses on POMC neurons while feeding leads to an increased expression of GluR2-lacking AMPARs on POMC neurons.
claims.source: This suggests that fasting facilitates GluR2-containing AMPAR translocation to synapses on POMC neurons while feeding leads to an increased expression of GluR2-lacking AMPARs on POMC neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the rectification data.

claims.claim: The AMPAR/NMDAR ratio was comparable in NPY/AgRP neurons between fasted and fed mice.
claims.source: The AMPAR/NMDAR ratio (fasting, 3.427 ± 0.820, n = 6; feeding, 5.818 ± 1.891, n = 4, p=0.29, unpaired T-test) and RI of AMPAR-EPSCs (fasting, 0.281 ± 0.071, n = 8; feeding, 0.211 ± 0.051, n = 6, p=0.44, unpaired T-test) were comparable in NPY/AgRP neurons between fasted and fed mice (Figure 3)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: The RI of AMPAR-EPSCs was comparable in NPY/AgRP neurons between fasted and fed mice.
claims.source: The AMPAR/NMDAR ratio (fasting, 3.427 ± 0.820, n = 6; feeding, 5.818 ± 1.891, n = 4, p=0.29, unpaired T-test) and RI of AMPAR-EPSCs (fasting, 0.281 ± 0.071, n = 8; feeding, 0.211 ± 0.051, n = 6, p=0.44, unpaired T-test) were comparable in NPY/AgRP neurons between fasted and fed mice (Figure 3)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: The change in the composition of AMPARs is selective to POMC neurons during different mouse feeding paradigms.
claims.source: To test whether the change in the composition of AMPARs is selective to POMC neurons during the different mouse feeding paradigms, we examined the AMPAR/NMDAR ratio and rectification of AMPAR-EPSCs in neighboring NPY/AgRP neurons of fasted and fed mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison between POMC and NPY/AgRP neurons.

claims.claim: The normalized eEPSC amplitudes were 84.3 ± 5.6% of baseline (n = 8) in fasted mice and 69.3 ± 5.3% of baseline (n = 7) in fed mice after IEM 1460 application.
claims.source: The normalized eEPSC amplitudes were 84.3 ± 5.6% of baseline (n = 8) in fasted mice and 69.3 ± 5.3% of baseline (n = 7) in fed mice
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: The inhibition of EPSC amplitude in POMC neurons induced by IEM 1460 was significantly greater in fed than fasted mice.
claims.source: the inhibition of EPSC amplitude in POMC neurons induced by IEM 1460 was significantly greater in fed than fasted mice (p<0.05, unpaired one-tail T-test) (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: There are more GluR2-lacking AMPARs in POMC neurons in fed versus fasted mice.
claims.source: This observation supports the premise that there are more GluR2-lacking AMPARs in POMC neurons in fed versus fasted mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference from the IEM 1460 experiment.

claims.claim: The median and distribution of mEPSC amplitude was not significantly different between normal and Ca2+-free ACSF in POMC neurons of fasted mice.
claims.source: In POMC neurons of fasted mice, the median and distribution of mEPSC amplitude was not significantly different between normal and Ca2+-free ACSF (normal ACSF, 13.46 ± 0.65 pA, n = 13; Ca2+-free ACSF, 11.64 ± 0.787, n = 9) (Figures 1a,c and 5a,b)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: The averaged median and distribution of mEPSC amplitude was significantly decreased in Ca2+-free ACSF than in normal ACSF in POMC neurons from fed mice.
claims.source: while the averaged median and distribution of mEPSC amplitude was significantly decreased in Ca2+ -free ACSF than in normal ACSF in POMC neurons from fed mice (normal ACSF, 16.37 ± 1.55 pA, n = 14; Ca2+-free ACSF, 10.93 ± 0.4866 pA, n = 9, p<0.05 unpaired t-test) (Figures 1a,c and 5a,b).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Averaged median and distribution of mEPSC amplitudes without extracellular calcium were not significantly different between POMC neurons of fed and fasted groups.
claims.source: Notably, averaged median and distribution of mEPSC amplitudes without extracellular calcium were not significantly different between POMC neurons of fed and fasted groups [p=0.456 for average mEPSC amplitude (unpaired T-test), p=0.70 for distribution (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test)] (Figure 5c,d)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Extracellular calcium ions contribute more to the amplitude of mEPSCs in POMC neurons of fed but not fasted mice.
claims.source: indicating that extracellular calcium ions contribute more to the amplitude of mEPSCs in POMC neurons of fed but not fasted mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference from the calcium-free ACSF experiments.

claims.claim: The calcium-free ACSF results are consistent with GluR2 entry into the synapses in the fasted state.
claims.source: This is consistent with GluR2 entry into the synapses in the fasted state.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference connecting the experimental results to the hypothesis about GluR2 entry.

claims.claim: In fed mice, β endorphin secretion significantly increased in hypothalamic slices treated with AMPA compared to aCSF, AMPA + IEM 1460 and IEM 1460.
claims.source: In fed mice, β endorphin secretion significantly increased in hypothalamic slices treated with AMPA compared to aCSF, AMPA + the Cp-AMPA blocker IEM 1460 and IEM 1460 (Figure 6a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from beta-endorphin secretion assays.

claims.claim: In fasted mice, β endorphin levels were comparable in hypothalamic slices treated with AMPA compared to aCSF, AMPA + IEM 1460 and IEM 1460.
claims.source: In fasted mice, β endorphin levels were comparable in hypothalamic slices treated with AMPA compared to aCSF, AMPA + IEM 1460 and IEM 1460 (Figure 6b).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from beta-endorphin secretion assays.

claims.claim: β endorphin could be released via activation of Cp-AMPAR, which is dominant in POMC neurons under fed condition.
claims.source: This suggests that β endorphin could be released via activation of Cp-AMPAR, which is dominant in POMC neurons under fed condition.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference from the beta-endorphin secretion experiments.

claims.claim: The RI was 0.34 ± 0.04 (n = 8) in POMC neurons of the ARC of HFD fed mice and 0.46 ± 0.03 (n = 9) in ND fed mice.
claims.source: The RI was 0.34 ± 0.04 (n = 8) in POMC neurons of the ARC of HFD fed mice and 0.46 ± 0.03 (n = 9) in ND fed mice. This represents a significant difference in RI (p<0.01, T-test, Figure 7c) between these two groups
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: The rectification of AMPAR-EPSCs was significantly enhanced in HFD mice compared to ND mice.
claims.source: This represents a significant difference in RI (p<0.01, T-test, Figure 7c) between these two groups, suggesting that the rectification of AMPAR-EPSCs was significantly enhanced in HFD mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the RI data from HFD vs ND mice.

claims.claim: Cp-AMPAR expression at synaptic sites on POMC neurons is enhanced by HFD.
claims.source: These data indicate that Cp-AMPAR expression at synaptic sites on POMC neurons is enhanced by HFD.
claims.evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the HFD rectification data.

claims.claim: The mEPSC amplitude decreased after removing extracellular calcium in POMC neurons in both HFD and ND conditions.
claims.source: The mEPSC amplitude decreased after removing extracellular calcium in POMC neurons in both HFDs [Ca2+ present: 15.91 ± 2.17, Ca2+, absent: 12.39 ± 1.33 pA (mean ± SEM), p<0.05 for averaged median amplitude (paired T-test), p<0.001 for distribution (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test), n = 8, Figure 6d,e] and ND conditions [Ca2+ present: 16.06 ± 1.05, Ca2+ absent: 14.19 ± 1.27 pA (mean ± SEM), p<0.05 for averaged median amplitude (paired T-test), p<0.001 for distribution (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test), n = 8, Figure 7f,g].
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: mEPSC amplitude without Ca2+ was smaller in HFD mice compared to ND.
claims.source: Interestingly, mEPSC amplitude without Ca2+ was smaller in HFD mice compared to ND [p<0.001 for distribution (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test) Figure 6e]
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: mEPSC amplitude with Ca2+ did not show a significant difference between HFD and ND groups.
claims.source: whereas those with Ca2+ did not show a significant difference between the two groups [p=0.56 for distribution (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test) Figure 7f,g].
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Short-term HFD application induces higher calcium permeability through Cp-AMPAR expression on POMC neurons more than ND does.
claims.source: These data suggest that short-term HFD application induces higher calcium permeability through Cp-AMPAR expression on POMC neurons more than ND does.
claims.evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the HFD calcium-free ACSF experiments.

claims.claim: The RI was 0.489 ± 0.062 (n = 8) in fasted plus saline-treated mice, but significantly less in the fasted plus leptin-treated mice: 0.296 ± 0.057 (n = 7).
claims.source: The RI was 0.489 ± 0.062 (n = 8) in fasted plus saline-treated mice, but significantly less in the fasted plus leptin-treated mice: 0.296 ± 0.057 (n = 7). (Figure 8b,c).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: The RI was 0.585 ± 0.050 (n = 3) without leptin treatment and 0.212 ± 0.063 (n = 3) with leptin treatment in slices from fasted mice.
claims.source: The RI was 0.585 ± 0.050 (n = 3) without leptin treatment and 0.212 ± 0.063 (n = 3) with leptin treatment in slices from fasted mice, thus showing a significantly smaller RI in leptin-treated POMC neurons compared to the control and systemic leptin application (Figure 8d,e).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro leptin treatment.

claims.claim: Leptin treatment showed a significantly smaller RI in leptin-treated POMC neurons compared to the control and systemic leptin application.
claims.source: The RI was 0.585 ± 0.050 (n = 3) without leptin treatment and 0.212 ± 0.063 (n = 3) with leptin treatment in slices from fasted mice, thus showing a significantly smaller RI in leptin-treated POMC neurons compared to the control and systemic leptin application (Figure 8d,e).
claims.evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the in vitro leptin treatment data.

claims.claim: Rapamycin treatment caused a significant increase in the RI in POMC neurons compared to saline injected fed mice.
claims.source: Rapamycin treatment caused a significant increase in the RI in POMC neurons compared to saline injected fed mice [rapamycin group: 0.817 ± 0.104 (n = 7), saline group: 0.403 ± 0.066 (n = 7)] (Figure 9a–c).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: The ARC slices from fasted mice incubated with 100 µM leucine for 4 hr showed a significant decrease in RI.
claims.source: Furthermore, the ARC slices from fasted mice incubated with 100 µM leucine (an activator of mTOR) for 4 hr showed a significant decrease in RI [leucine group: 0.301 ± 0.033 (n = 6), control group: 0.498 ± 0.449 (n = 6), p<0.01, T-test)] (Figure 10).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: The leptin-mTOR pathway contributes to the enhanced expression of Cp-AMPARs in POMC neurons in the state of positive energy balance.
claims.source: These results provide evidence that the leptin-mTOR pathway contributes to the enhanced expression of Cp-AMPARs in POMC neurons in the state of positive energy balance (fed animals).
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference from the rapamycin and leucine experiments.

claims.claim: The RI on the fed group did not show a significant difference between the control at 10 or 15 min after rupture of the membrane with PD98095 treatment.
claims.source: The RI on the fed group did not show a significant difference between the control at 10 or 15 min after rupture of the membrane.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ERK inhibitor experiments.

claims.claim: The RI on the fasted group decreased significantly at 10 min after rupture with PD98095 treatment.
claims.source: By comparison, the RI on the fasted group decreased significantly at 10 min after rupture [fasted group: 0.60 ± 0.098 at 1 min, 0.353 ± 0.038 at 10 min, 0.344 ± 0.048 at 15 min, (n = 7) p<0.01 in 1 min vs. 10 min and 1 min vs. 15 min (two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) and Tukey multiple comparison posthoc test), fed group: 0.426 ± 0.064 at 1 min, 0.409 ± 0.068 at 10 min, 0.332 ± 0.051 at 15 min (n = 7)] (Figure 11a–c).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: ERK phosphorylation promotes GluR2-containing Ci-AMPAR translocation to the synaptic membrane.
claims.source: These data suggest that ERK phosphorylation promotes GluR2-containing Ci-AMPAR translocation to the synaptic membrane.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference from the ERK inhibitor experiments.

claims.claim: mEPSC amplitude which reflects efficiency of the synaptic transmission at the postsynaptic site is higher in POMC neurons in the ARC in fed animals than in fasted animals.
claims.source: In this study, we showed that mEPSC amplitude which reflects efficiency of the synaptic transmission at the postsynaptic site is higher in POMC neurons in the ARC in fed animals than in fasted animals
claims.evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the mEPSC data.

claims.claim: Under a normal feeding paradigm a higher efficiency of glutamatergic transmission onto POMC neurons may lead to the activation of POMC neurons.
claims.source: suggesting that under a normal feeding paradigm a higher efficiency of glutamatergic transmission onto POMC neurons may lead to the activation of POMC neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a potential consequence of the observed higher mEPSC amplitude.

claims.claim: More GluR2-lacking, Ca2+-permeable AMPARs are expressed on the surface of POMC neurons in animals under normal feeding and HFD.
claims.source: Therefore, our results demonstrate that more GluR2-lacking, Ca2+-permeable AMPARs are expressed on the surface of POMC neurons in animals under normal feeding and HFD.
claims.evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results.

claims.claim: GluR1 but not GluR2 is expressed in ARC neurons under a normal feeding paradigm.
claims.source: This is consistent with a previous study showing that GluR1 but not GluR2 is expressed in ARC neurons under a normal feeding paradigm (Bowie and Mayer, 1995; Gao et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: GluR2 is not expressed in certain types of neurons in many brain areas under basal conditions.
claims.source: There is ample evidence that GluR2 is not expressed in certain types of neurons in many brain areas, including neocortical, hippocampal, and amygdaloidal fast-spiking interneurons, cerebellar stellate cells, dorsal horn interneurons, large striatal cholinergic neurons, bushy and stellate cells of the cochlear nucleus, spinothalamic projection neurons, and retinal amacrine cells, in addition to Bergmann glia and oligodendrocyte precursor cells of the cerebellum under basal conditions.
claims.evidence: This claim draws from established scientific knowledge about GluR2 expression patterns.

claims.claim: Dendrites of POMC neurons were aspiny.
claims.source: Studies showed that dendrites of POMC neurons were aspiny (Hentges et al., 2005; Isaac et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2012)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Cerebellar stellate cells express Cp-AMPAR-dependent and NMDAR-independent LTD after high-frequency stimulation.
claims.source: For example, cerebellar stellate cells express Cp-AMPAR-dependent and NMDAR-independent LTD after high-frequency stimulation, which includes the replacement of Cp-AMPARs by Ca2+-impermeable GluR2-containing AMPARs after the expression of LTD (Liu and Cull-Candy, 2000).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: The depletion of NMDARs specifically in POMC neurons did not have a significant effect on feeding and energy expenditure in animals.
claims.source: It is important to note that in a recent study, the depletion of NMDARs specifically in POMC neurons did not have a significant effect on feeding and energy expenditure in animals, suggesting that NMDARs may not be required for the functions exerted by POMC neurons (Liu et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: NMDARs may not be required for the functions exerted by POMC neurons.
claims.source: It is important to note that in a recent study, the depletion of NMDARs specifically in POMC neurons did not have a significant effect on feeding and energy expenditure in animals, suggesting that NMDARs may not be required for the functions exerted by POMC neurons (Liu et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference from the cited study on NMDAR depletion.

claims.claim: HFD did not induce weight change until at least 2 weeks after starting it.
claims.source: Under these conditions, it is expected that the secondary effects originating from obesity by HFD application were minimized, because HFD did not induce weight change until at least 2 weeks after starting it (Lin et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: Circulating levels of leptin have been reported to increase at 3 days after HFD application.
claims.source: Circulating levels of leptin have been reported to increase at 3 days after HFD application (Wang et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: POMC neurons were rewired in a polysialic acid molecule-dependent fashion during HFD, and showed increasing frequency of EPSCs but no change in amplitude of PSCs.
claims.source: In this period, POMC neurons were rewired in a polysialic acid molecule-dependent fashion, and showed increasing frequency of EPSCs but no change in amplitude of PSCs (Benani et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: The levels of circulating leptin decline under fasting conditions.
claims.source: Under fasting conditions, the levels of circulating leptin decline, leading to a reduction in the number and efficacy of excitatory inputs onto POMC neurons (Ahima et al., 1996; Pinto et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Fasting leads to a reduction in the number and efficacy of excitatory inputs onto POMC neurons.
claims.source: Under fasting conditions, the levels of circulating leptin decline, leading to a reduction in the number and efficacy of excitatory inputs onto POMC neurons (Ahima et al., 1996; Pinto et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Leptin promotes the expression of GluR2-lacking Ca2+-permeable AMPARs at the postsynaptic site.
claims.source: Thus, leptin promotes the expression of GluR2-lacking Ca2+-permeable AMPARs at the postsynaptic site.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference from the leptin treatment experiments.

claims.claim: mTOR was shown to be downstream of the leptin signal via PI3K pathway, in order to suppress food intake and regulate POMC expression in the hypothalamus.
claims.source: mTOR was shown to be downstream of the leptin signal via PI3K pathway, in order to suppress food intake and regulate POMC expression in the hypothalamus (Blouet et al., 2009; Cota et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Leptin directly regulates Cp-AMPAR translocation by increasing GluR1 expression at synapses of hippocampal CA1 neurons via PTEN inhibition and activation of the PI3K pathway.
claims.source: There is also evidence that leptin directly regulates Cp-AMPAR translocation by increasing GluR1 expression at synapses of hippocampal CA1 neurons via PTEN inhibition and activation of the PI3K pathway (Moult et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: Leptin removed Cp-AMPARs after LTP induction via calcium/calmodulin-dependent phosphatase and calcinurin at certain time points after induction of LTP.
claims.source: Leptin also removed Cp-AMPARs after LTP induction via calcium/calmodulin-dependent phosphatase and calcinurin at certain time points after induction of LTP (Moult et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: mTOR-mediated protein translation is needed to establish several types of long-lasting synaptic changes and long-term memory.
claims.source: Additionally, growing evidence has shown that mTOR-mediated protein translation is needed to establish several types of long-lasting synaptic changes and long-term memory (see review [Costa-Mattioli et al., 2009]).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claims.claim: Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) induced GluR1 translation that required mTOR activation in hippocampal CA1 neurons.
claims.source: For example, brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), which is essential for LTP, induced GluR1 translation that required mTOR activation in hippocampal CA1 neurons (Fortin et al., 2012; Slipczuk et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: mTOR-mediated autophagy controls the GluR1 subunit.
claims.source: Furthermore, a recent study suggested that mTOR-mediated autophagy control of the GluR1 subunit (Shehata et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: Autophagy in POMC neurons maintained neurite growth.
claims.source: These data, taken together with a recent report that autophagy in POMC neurons maintained neurite growth (Coupé et al., 2012)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: mTOR may regulate AMPAR turnover at the postsynaptic site of POMC neurons to regulate feeding activity.
claims.source: indicates that mTOR may regulate AMPAR turnover at the postsynaptic site of POMC neurons to regulate feeding activity.
claims.evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a potential mechanism based on cited literature and current findings.

claims.claim: Fasting increases glucocorticoid which also regulates mTOR.
claims.source: Fasting not only induces a decline in leptin but also increases glucocorticoid (Champy et al., 2004) which also regulates mTOR (Polman et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Glucocorticoid decreases POMC mRNA expression.
claims.source: Glucocorticoid decreases POMC mRNA expression, and moreover, it regulates synaptic plasticity in the hippocampus (Popoli et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: Glucocorticoid regulates synaptic plasticity in the hippocampus.
claims.source: Glucocorticoid decreases POMC mRNA expression, and moreover, it regulates synaptic plasticity in the hippocampus (Popoli et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: A decline in glucocorticoid after adrenalectomy did not alter the amplitude of mEPSCs onto POMC neurons.
claims.source: However, a decline in glucocorticoid after adrenalectomy did not alter the amplitude of mEPSCs onto POMC neurons, although it depolarized POMC neurons and increased the frequency of mEPSCs (Gyengesi et al., 2010)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: Glucocorticoid does not likely regulate translocation of AMPARs in POMC neurons.
claims.source: However, a decline in glucocorticoid after adrenalectomy did not alter the amplitude of mEPSCs onto POMC neurons, although it depolarized POMC neurons and increased the frequency of mEPSCs (Gyengesi et al., 2010), suggesting that it does not likely regulate translocation of AMPARs in POMC neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference from the cited study on adrenalectomy.

claims.claim: ERK may promote Ci-AMPAR translocation to the synaptic membrane of POMC neurons during the fasted but not fed states.
claims.source: We also observed that inhibition of ERK decreased the RI increased by fasting, which indicates that ERK may promote Ci-AMPAR translocation to the synaptic membrane of POMC neurons during the fasted but not fed states.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference from the ERK inhibitor experiments.

claims.claim: ERK switches the AMPAR phenotype from Cp-AMPA to Ci-AMPA in several neurons including hippocampus, cortex and cerebellar stellate cells.
claims.source: This is consistent with the role of ERK to switch the AMPAR phenotype from Cp-AMPA to Ci-AMPA in several neurons including hippocampus, cortex (Schroeter et al., 2007), and cerebellar stellate cells (Liu et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: ERK phosphorylation was induced under the fasted but not fed state, and this phosphorylation was reversed by re-feeding.
claims.source: Our finding is also consistent with the observation that ERK phosphorylation was induced under the fasted but not fed state, and this phosphorylation was reversed by re-feeding (Morikawa et al., 2004; Ueyama et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Leptin induces ERK phosphorylation in the ARC.
claims.source: Although several lines of evidence suggest that leptin induces ERK phosphorylation in the ARC (Bjørbaek et al., 2001; Bouret et al., 2012)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: POMC neurons consist of two subpopulations; approximately half of these neurons showed high RI values (greater than 0.7) during fasting conditions, while the others displayed lower RI values within the range of 0.25–0.5.
claims.source: Our results suggest that POMC neurons consist of two subpopulations; approximately half of these neurons showed high RI values (greater than 0.7) during fasting conditions, while the others displayed lower RI values within the range of 0.25–0.5 which is similar to POMC neurons under a fed condition.
claims.evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the heterogeneity observed in the RI data.

claims.claim: POMC neurons with high RI under fasting conditions could be under the regulation of the leptin-mTOR pathway, whereas those with low RI could be leptin insensitive.
claims.source: POMC neurons with high RI under fasting conditions could be under the regulation of the leptin-mTOR pathway, whereas those with low RI could be leptin insensitive.
claims.evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a potential explanation for the observed heterogeneity.

claims.claim: A subset of POMC neurons respond to leptin but not serotonin while the other subset responds in the opposite way.
claims.source: This result is consistent with the evidence that a subset of POMC neurons respond to leptin but not serotonin while the other subset responds in the opposite way (Gao et al., 2017; Sohn et al., 2011)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: The modulation of glutamate receptor structure has been shown to be a key part of neuronal responses to changes in the external environment, including learning, memory, and drug addition.
claims.source: The modulation of glutamate receptor structure has been shown to be a key part of neuronal responses to changes in the external environment, including learning, memory, and drug addition.
claims.evidence: This claim draws from established scientific knowledge about glutamate receptor plasticity.

claims.claim: The results provide a feasible mechanistic explanation for long-term impairment of POMC neuronal functions on HFD in relation to calcium overload.
claims.source: Because our observations emphasize the importance of calcium entry into POMC neurons during their activation, our results provide a feasible mechanistic explanation for long-term impairment of POMC neuronal functions on HFD in relation to calcium overload (Paeger et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a potential mechanistic explanation based on the current findings and cited literature.

results.result: Fasting alters postsynaptic properties in POMC neurons, with mEPSC frequency remaining unchanged but amplitude distribution significantly differing between fasted and fed states. The averaged median amplitude tended to be smaller in fasted mice (13.46 ± 0.65 pA) compared to fed mice (16.37 ± 1.55 pA), though this did not reach statistical significance (p=0.10).
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C22 provide converging evidence from mEPSC recordings showing postsynaptic changes during fasting. While the mean amplitude difference was not statistically significant (C20), the significant difference in amplitude distribution (C21, p<0.001) supports altered postsynaptic properties (C22). The frequency data (C19) appropriately shows no change, focusing attention on postsynaptic mechanisms.

results.result: Food deprivation induces a more linear I-V relationship of AMPAR-EPSCs in POMC neurons compared to fed mice. The rectification index (RI) was significantly higher in fasted mice (0.59 ± 0.01) compared to fed mice (0.30 ± 0.03, p<0.05), indicating that feeding promotes expression of GluR2-lacking calcium-permeable AMPARs while fasting facilitates GluR2-containing AMPAR translocation.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C24-C27 present a coherent result supported by electrophysiological measurements of AMPAR rectification. The significant difference in RI between fasted and fed states (C25) is well-documented with appropriate statistics. The interpretation regarding GluR2 subunit composition (C27) is reasonable given the established relationship between rectification and GluR2 content, though it remains inferential.

results.result: The AMPAR/NMDAR ratio showed no significant difference between POMC neurons of fasted and fed animals (fasting: 1.672 ± 0.679, n=6; feeding: 1.415 ± 0.136, n=6, p=0.73).
results.evaluation: Claim C23 is supported by appropriate statistical analysis showing no difference in AMPAR/NMDAR ratio between feeding states. This negative result is important as it indicates that changes in AMPAR composition rather than overall AMPAR/NMDAR balance account for the observed differences.

results.result: The changes in AMPAR composition are selective to POMC neurons, as neighboring NPY/AgRP neurons showed no significant differences in AMPAR/NMDAR ratio or RI between fasted and fed states.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C30 provide important control data demonstrating cell-type specificity. The lack of changes in NPY/AgRP neurons (C28, C29) supports the inference that AMPAR compositional changes are selective to POMC neurons (C30). This strengthens the main findings by ruling out generalized effects.

results.result: IEM-1460, a selective Cp-AMPAR antagonist, significantly reduced EPSC amplitude in fed mice (69.3 ± 5.3% of baseline) more than in fasted mice (84.3 ± 5.6% of baseline, p<0.05), supporting the presence of more GluR2-lacking AMPARs in fed versus fasted POMC neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C31-C33 provide pharmacological validation of the rectification findings. The differential effect of IEM-1460 between feeding states (C32) with appropriate statistics supports the conclusion about GluR2-lacking AMPAR prevalence (C33). This orthogonal approach strengthens the main result.

results.result: Removal of extracellular calcium decreased mEPSC amplitude in fed (16.37 to 10.93 pA, p<0.05) but not fasted mice (13.46 to 11.64 pA), with no difference between groups in calcium-free conditions. This indicates greater calcium contribution to mEPSC amplitude in fed mice, consistent with GluR2 entry during fasting.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C34-C38 provide strong converging evidence using calcium manipulation. The differential effect of calcium removal between feeding states (C35 vs C34) and the equalization of amplitudes in calcium-free conditions (C36) logically support the interpretation about calcium permeability differences (C37, C38). The experimental design and statistics are appropriate.

results.result: β-endorphin secretion from hypothalamic slices significantly increased with AMPA treatment in fed but not fasted mice, and this increase was blocked by IEM-1460, suggesting that β-endorphin release occurs via Cp-AMPAR activation dominant in fed conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C41 demonstrate functional consequences of Cp-AMPAR expression. The differential AMPA-induced β-endorphin secretion between feeding states (C39 vs C40) and its blockade by IEM-1460 support the inference about Cp-AMPAR-mediated release (C41). However, the manuscript lacks detailed statistical analysis for this experiment.

results.result: Ten days of high-fat diet (HFD) exposure resulted in significantly enhanced AMPAR-EPSC rectification in POMC neurons (RI: 0.34 ± 0.04) compared to normal diet (RI: 0.46 ± 0.03, p<0.01), indicating increased Cp-AMPAR expression with HFD.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C6, C42-C44 extend the main findings to a positive energy balance model. The significant difference in RI between HFD and ND (C42) with appropriate statistics supports enhanced Cp-AMPAR expression (C44). The 10-day timeframe minimizes obesity-related confounds as discussed in the manuscript.

results.result: In both HFD and ND conditions, mEPSC amplitude decreased after calcium removal, but calcium-free amplitudes were smaller in HFD versus ND mice (p<0.001) while calcium-containing amplitudes were comparable (p=0.56), suggesting HFD induces higher calcium permeability through Cp-AMPARs.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C48 provide mechanistic insight into HFD effects using calcium manipulation. The pattern of results—decreased amplitude with calcium removal in both conditions (C45) but differential calcium-free amplitudes (C46) with similar calcium-containing amplitudes (C47)—logically supports increased calcium permeability in HFD (C48). Statistics are appropriate.

results.result: Leptin treatment significantly decreased RI in fasted mice both systemically (from 0.489 ± 0.062 to 0.296 ± 0.057) and in vitro (from 0.585 ± 0.050 to 0.212 ± 0.063), demonstrating that leptin promotes expression of GluR2-lacking Cp-AMPARs at postsynaptic sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C51, C72 demonstrate leptin's role in regulating AMPAR composition. Both in vivo (C49) and in vitro (C50, C51) leptin treatments show consistent effects on RI with appropriate statistics. The inference about leptin promoting Cp-AMPAR expression (C72) is well-supported by the data, though the in vitro experiment has small sample sizes (n=3).

results.result: Rapamycin (mTOR inhibitor) significantly increased RI in fed mice (0.817 ± 0.104 vs 0.403 ± 0.066), while leucine (mTOR activator) decreased RI in fasted mice (0.301 ± 0.033 vs 0.498 ± 0.449, p<0.01), indicating the leptin-mTOR pathway contributes to Cp-AMPAR expression in positive energy balance.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C54 identify mTOR as a downstream mediator of leptin's effects. The bidirectional manipulation of mTOR (inhibition with rapamycin in C52, activation with leucine in C53) producing opposite effects on RI provides strong mechanistic evidence. The inference about the leptin-mTOR pathway (C54) is well-supported by these complementary experiments.

results.result: ERK inhibition with PD98059 significantly decreased RI in fasted but not fed POMC neurons (fasted: 0.60 at 1 min to 0.353 at 10 min, p<0.01; fed: no significant change), suggesting ERK promotes GluR2-containing Ci-AMPAR translocation during fasting.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C57, C86 identify ERK as a regulator of AMPAR composition in the fasted state. The time-course experiment with appropriate statistics (C56) showing selective effects in fasted neurons (C55) supports the inference about ERK promoting Ci-AMPAR translocation (C57, C86). The experimental design using intracellular inhibitor application is appropriate.

results.result: The authors conclude that mEPSC amplitude is higher in fed than fasted POMC neurons, reflecting greater synaptic transmission efficiency that may activate POMC neurons under normal feeding, with more GluR2-lacking Cp-AMPARs expressed in fed and HFD conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C60 represent summary interpretations. While C58 is supported by the mEPSC data, C59 is speculative about functional consequences without direct activity measurements. C60 summarizes multiple findings but the claim about "higher" amplitude in C58 conflicts with the non-significant difference reported in C20 (p=0.10), creating internal inconsistency.

results.result: The authors propose that calcium entry via Cp-AMPARs is inherent to POMC neuron activation and may underlie vulnerability to calcium overload during sustained activation in over-nutrition, providing a mechanistic explanation for long-term POMC neuronal impairment on HFD.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C8, C94 represent speculative conclusions about pathophysiological implications. While the data support calcium entry via Cp-AMPARs (C7), the claims about vulnerability to calcium overload (C8) and long-term impairment (C94) are not directly tested. No calcium imaging, cell viability, or long-term functional assessments are provided to support these speculations.

results.result: The authors suggest POMC neurons consist of two subpopulations based on RI heterogeneity during fasting, with high-RI neurons potentially regulated by leptin-mTOR pathway and low-RI neurons possibly leptin-insensitive.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C91 propose POMC neuron heterogeneity based on observed RI variability. While C90 describes the observation, C91 is highly speculative without direct evidence. No experiments specifically test leptin sensitivity in identified subpopulations or correlate RI values with leptin responsiveness in individual neurons.
